vision: Aerodrome Finance bindings, Sugar-backed reads, a built-in price layer, and denominator-honest analytics for Elixir on Base (chain 8453). Correctness is graded by deployed contracts, never by our own encoders. Part of the seven-repository onchain family, built on the onchain core library.

bindings.description: Typed eth_call wrappers over the nine captured ABIs, including the count()-driven LpSugar pagination driver.

evidence_release.description: ABI drift detection, live end-to-end proof across two endpoints, and the 0.1.0 hex release checklist.

foundations.description: The layer gate that makes 'analytics never touches the network' checkable, weekly-epoch arithmetic, the decode strategy, pinned-block golden fixtures, and the multi-endpoint portability seam.

math.description: Pure integer tick, liquidity, stable-invariant and price math, differentially graded against the deployed SlipstreamHelper and a real v2 pool.

price.description: Price resolution split on the pure/impure seam: route math in analytics, Chainlink anchors and materialisation in the read layer.

read_api.description: The ergonomic Sugar.* consumer surface, re-proving the pagination invariant at the layer where a naive rewrite would reintroduce it.

types.description: Structs for every Sugar tuple shape, each carrying an ABI field-count/order drift test — the defence positional decode requires.

write.description: Router/Gauge/NFPM/Voter calldata builders with signing opt-in, graded by an independent encoder and real deployed reverts.

acceptance_criteria: deps in .reach.exs uses mode: :allowlist with an explicit allowed: entry per declared layer (types -> [], base -> [], bindings -> [:types, :base], analytics -> [:types, :base], read -> [:types, :base, :bindings, :analytics], write -> everything below); the forbidden list is gone

A .reach.exs comment records that Mix.Tasks.* is intentionally outside the layer graph because the fixture generators must reach the network

CLAUDE.md's layer-contract section is corrected to describe what the gate actually enforces, its dependency table stops presenting Onchain.Solidity and Onchain.Contract.Generator as runtime-available (they live in onchain_evm, dev/test only), and AGENTS.md is regenerated so mix agents.check passes

Adding anything to a smells ignore list; smell findings are fixed, never ignored

task.body:
CLAUDE.md asserts that mix reach.check --arch fails the build when an analytics module makes an RPC call. Verify that claim before changing anything: it is false as configured, and the entire analytics-is-testable-with-zero-network guarantee rests on it.

Two concrete defects, both readable in deps/reach/lib/reach/check/architecture.ex.

First, layer_graph/2 only emits an edge when BOTH caller and callee resolve to a declared layer (module_layer(callee, layers); nil drops the edge). Onchain.RPC, Onchain.Contract, Onchain.Multicall and Req belong to no declared layer, so a direct RPC call from analytics produces zero violations.

Second, forbidden_dependency_rule_matches?({from, to}, edge) reads as layer from must not call layer to. {:analytics, :bindings} is missing from the forbidden list, so analytics may call bindings freely, which is a second network path. And {:bindings, :types} IS present, which forbids exactly the dependency the documented layer table requires; it will block every bindings task until fixed.

Convert deps to mode: :allowlist and enumerate what each layer may reach. An allowlist is exhaustive by construction, so a future layer cannot silently open a hole. Then add calls: [forbidden: ...] for the out-of-layer network modules. Reach.Config.valid_forbidden_calls?/1 accepts {caller_patterns, call_patterns} and {caller_patterns, call_patterns, except: [...]} with glob strings.

Evaluate, do not assume, whether effects: [by_layer: [analytics: [:pure, :exception]]] is usable. Reach.Effects.classify/2 falls back to :unknown for unresolvable calls and the architecture check subtracts the allowed list from function_effects/2, which includes :unknown. If :unknown floods the report, drop the effects policy and record in a .reach.exs comment why the forbidden-calls rule is the load-bearing mechanism instead. Do not ship a noisy gate.

Prove each rule by introducing the violating line, capturing the failure output, and reverting. A gate nobody has seen fail is not a gate.

OPEN DECISIONS settled 2026-08-26 (do not re-ask): (a) types is forbidden from reaching base — Types are pure structs and the table's "depends on nothing" is the allowlist; (b) Onchain.Aerodrome.Contracts and Math.* stay one `base` layer, because analytics must reach Contracts.constants() and same-layer edges are exempt.

AUTHORITY: deps/reach/lib/reach/check/architecture.ex and deps/reach/lib/reach/config.ex in this checkout are the authority on what the gate enforces. Not CLAUDE.md, not the reach README. Read the matcher functions before writing config.

Epoch.epochs_per_year/0 returns the integer 52, and its @doc states that 52 * 604_800 is about 364 days and that this is the annualiser Analytics.APR uses, because annualising from a daily rate overstates by roughly 7x
start/1, end/1, next/1, previous/1, index/1, bounds/1, contains?/2, range/2 and seconds_remaining/1 are exported with @spec and doctests
Epoch.end/1 is documented as exclusive (the start of the next epoch) and a test asserts contains?(Epoch.end(ts), ts) is false — an off-by-one here silently double-counts an epoch of emissions
range(from_ts, to_ts) returns epoch starts ascending, inclusive of the epoch containing from_ts, and returns [] when to_ts precedes from_ts rather than raising
A test asserts Epoch.start(t) equals Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds * div(t, Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds) so the constant is never forked into a second literal
Negative and pre-1970 timestamps return {:error, {:timestamp_out_of_range, ts}} rather than a negative epoch index
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Any RPC read of epoch state; RewardsSugar.epochsByAddress belongs to the read layer
The LpEpoch struct, which is task 7
Timezone handling beyond UTC — Aerodrome epochs are UTC-only
task.body:
Pure weekly-epoch arithmetic for Aerodrome's ve(3,3) schedule. Epoch length is 604_800 seconds and epochs flip Thursday 00:00 UTC — not because of a hardcoded offset, but because Unix epoch 0 was itself a Thursday, so floor(ts / 604_800) * 604_800 lands on Thursday midnight with no correction term. Do not add an offset constant; if you feel the need to, your test timestamps are wrong.

The read layer will consume range/2 to build the epoch series for RewardsSugar.epochsByAddress pagination, and Analytics.APR will consume epochs_per_year/0 as its annualiser. Those two are this module's contract with the rest of the package; keep them stable and say so in the moduledoc.

This module is claimed by the analytics lane. No other module may define a second epoch helper; if a caller needs epoch boundaries, it calls here. Epoch is already declared in the base layer of .reach.exs, so it may depend on nothing but Onchain.Aerodrome.Contracts.

OPEN DECISION settled 2026-08-26 (do not re-ask): index/1 is an absolute epoch number since the Unix epoch. It is large, stable, and joins cleanly against on-chain data. Do not pin an Aerodrome genesis timestamp. Record that choice in the moduledoc.

AUTHORITY: the deployed RewardsSugar at 0x1b121EfDaF4ABb8785a315C51D29BCE0552A7678. cast call WEEK()(uint256) returned 604800 on 2026-08-26, recorded as check 6 in priv/abis/README.md. That contract, not a calendar library, defines the epoch length. If WEEK() ever disagrees with Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds, the contract wins.

acceptance_criteria: Bindings.Abi.signature/2 and Bindings.Abi.return_type/2 produce canonical Solidity type strings for every function in all nine priv/abis/*.json files, handling address, string, bool, uintN, intN, tuple, tuple[], type[] and type[N]

task.body:
Settle the decode strategy for the whole package in one place, then build the plumbing every binding task consumes.

The reachability fact this task exists to encode: hieroglyph 1.7.0 is a runtime dependency and its ABI.decode/3 does support decode_structs: true, which returns a map keyed by snake_case atoms. But hex-released onchain 0.13.0 exposes Onchain.Contract.call/5 and Onchain.ABI.decode_response/2 at 2-arity with no opts forwarding, so decode_structs cannot be reached through the project's own wrappers. Reaching past them straight into hieroglyph would mean bypassing our own abstraction, and decode_structs additionally raises at runtime on any un-interned field atom. Verify the arities yourself in deps/onchain before building on this.

Therefore: positional decode. Onchain.RPC.eth_call plus Onchain.ABI.decode_response(return_type, hex), then a hand-written from_raw/1 per struct in tasks 6 and 7. This is the shape onchain_aave already uses in production. It sidesteps atom interning entirely, because defstruct field atoms are literal source and nothing calls String.to_existing_atom/1 on dynamic input. The residual risk is silent field-order drift on a Sugar redeploy, which tasks 6 and 7 defend with per-struct field-count and order tests read directly from the ABI JSON.

Build Bindings.Abi: given an ABI file and a function name, return the canonical call signature and the canonical return-type signature by walking inputs, outputs and components recursively with Jason. Cache per file in a module attribute with @external_resource so a re-captured ABI forces a recompile.

Write the atom-interning demonstration test. It is the standing defence against a future engineer helpfully adding decode_structs: true somewhere it will raise in production.

CLAUDE.md, priv/abis/README.md and the README ABI paragraph currently still tell implementers to intern field atoms for decode_structs: true. That is the discarded path. Correct those three files in this task so a dispatched agent loading CLAUDE.md first does not follow it. Named tuple components in the Sourcify captures remain useful — they are the input to the field-order drift tests in tasks 6 and 7, not a reason to call decode_structs. Regenerating AGENTS.md is required because mix agents.check diffs it against CLAUDE.md.

OPEN DECISIONS settled 2026-08-26 (do not re-ask): (a) there is no runtime dependency on an unreleased onchain fix — mix.exs is hex-only, no path or git deps; (b) the type-string builder covers exactly what the nine captured ABIs need, not a general Solidity grammar.

AUTHORITY: priv/abis/lp_sugar.json and the other eight captured ABIs (Sourcify v2, deployed bytecode, named tuple components) are the sole source of truth for every signature. Not velodrome-finance/sugar's README, which is proven stale — it documents all(limit, offset) while the deployed contract is all(uint256,uint256,uint256) and the two-argument form reverts.

task.body:
Capture real eth_call response hex for every Sugar read function at one pinned Base block, commit it, and build the loader that tests consume. This is the package's only defence against Sugar redeploy drift once bindings land: a decode that starts returning nil or misaligned fields against these fixtures is drift, not a flaky test.

The capture tool needs a live BASE_RPC_URL (falling back to https://mainnet.base.org per the README) and is explicitly not part of mix ci — it is a dev workflow. What mix ci exercises is the committed fixtures plus the loader, with zero network.

Pin the block explicitly on every call. A fixture captured at latest is not a fixture; it is a snapshot of an unrecorded moment, and it makes every later mismatch unattributable.

Make sure at least one all(500, offset, non_zero_filter) capture returns fewer than 500 rows. That single fixture is what makes task 8's pagination-trap regression test possible, and without it that test can only assert the happy path.

AUTHORITY: live eth_call responses from the addresses in lib/onchain/aerodrome/contracts.ex, captured yourself at a block you record in the manifest. Not any remembered Sugar response shape, and not the Sourcify ABI alone — the ABI gives you the shape, not real field values to sanity-check against (for example that Lp.type really does take -1, 0 and positive values in practice).

task.body:
node-portability.md names this gap explicitly: no multi-endpoint test seam exists yet, and whoever builds one builds it first. Build it locally in this repo, not in onchain core, so every read and write integration test here can assert portability instead of it being a manual step that is easy to skip.

Model it on onchain core's existing single-endpoint Onchain.RPCCase but generalise to two named endpoints plus a helper that runs the same closure against both. Note that test/support is already on elixirc_paths(:test) in mix.exs, so no build config change is needed.

Never skip on a missing endpoint. A suite that reports zero failures from zero tests is a lie; flunk with the exact export command.

AUTHORITY: the public https://mainnet.base.org endpoint and a genuinely separate hosted provider of Alchemy or Infura class are the two authorities. Agreement between them, not agreement with our own archive node, is what portable means. Our node's ok result is not evidence; a hosted endpoint's real refusal is.

task.body:
Define the four structs the pool and token read surface decodes into. They are one task because they share one load-bearing invariant, not because they are each small: positional decode means ABI source order is semantic, so every one of them carries the same field-count and order drift test, and one reviewer verifies that pattern once across a single coherent diff.

Do not reorder fields for readability. Under positional decode, order is the contract.

The drift test is what replaces decode_structs entirely (see task 3's decision). It is the thing that actually protects against a Sugar redeploy quietly reordering Lp's fields, and it must read the JSON itself rather than going through Bindings.Abi, because a Types.* module and its test must not depend on the bindings layer.

Types.Token is shared across two ABIs. Confirm the shapes are byte-identical with a test; if a future capture makes them diverge, that test is where it surfaces.

task.body:
Define the five structs the veAERO side decodes into. They are one task because they share the same positional-decode drift invariant and the same fixture set, and because two of them share a nested type that must be defined exactly once.

Two shape facts to get right, both verified against the captured ABIs rather than inferred. Types.Vote ({lp, weight}) is byte-identical between VeSugar's VeNFT.votes and RelaySugar's Relay.votes, so it is defined once and aliased. And Relay is materially larger than its function count suggests: a wide struct with two nested arrays, one of them ({id, amount, earned}) unique to it. Record in the moduledoc that the field list is read from the ABI JSON, so nobody re-derives it from memory or from the function count later.

LpEpoch's bribes and fees are {token, amount} pairs; Reward is a flat six-field record. They are not structurally related. Do not merge their field lists.

task.title: Bindings.LpSugar — the full read surface and the count()-driven pagination driver
acceptance_criteria: count/1 and single-page all/4 (limit, offset, filter) are implemented via Onchain.RPC.eth_call plus a Bindings.Abi-derived signature, decoding positionally into [%Types.Lp{}]

The pagination driver drives offset TO count(), never terminating on a short page; a test using the task-4 non-zero-filter fixture (which returns fewer than limit rows mid-sequence) asserts the loop CONTINUES past that short page and the final offset reached equals or exceeds count()

An explicit anti-regression test encodes the bug by name: a naive stop-when-length(page)-is-less-than-limit implementation is asserted to UNDER-COUNT against the same fixture set, so the suite fails against the bug this task exists to prevent rather than merely passing against the fix

forSwaps/3, positions/4, positionsByFactory/5, positionsUnstakedConcentrated/4, tokens/5 and almEstimateAmounts/4 are implemented, decoding into [%Types.Swap{}], [%Types.Position{}], [%Types.Token{}] and a three-element amount tuple respectively

Each of those functions carries an @doc naming which index space its offset walks and the correct termination rule. positions, positionsByFactory, positionsUnstakedConcentrated, forSwaps and tokens iterate a SCANNED index space (pool index or NFT index) that is not the returned-row space — entries are filtered, deduplicated or skipped upstream, so a page shorter than limit is normal mid-enumeration and short-page termination is the same silent-data-loss bug as on all/4; enumeration ends only when the offset has walked the full scanned space. A pagination test consumes the task-4 positions short-page fixture and asserts enumeration CONTINUES past the short page

The filter argument on all/4 is an opaque non_neg_integer passthrough with an @doc warning that its semantics are undocumented upstream and that fixture drift detection is the only available verification
Decode correctness is proven against the task-4 fixtures for every function
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: The ergonomic Sugar.Pools wrapper, which is task 23

The MAX_* cap getters and the internal wiring getters (voter, registry, convertor, cl_helper, alm_factory, alm_map, launcher_map, token_sugar, lp_helper, locker_factory_map) — Contracts.constants() carries the verified pagination caps; further caps the ABI exposes (MAX_FACTORIES, MAX_ITERATIONS) are deliberately unwired, and re-fetching any of them live adds no v0.1 value
Analytics of any kind
task.body:
This is the highest-risk read task in the package, and the risk is a silent one.

LpSugar.all/3 applies its filter argument AFTER fetching the page. With a non-zero filter a full page returns fewer than limit rows while offset still indexes the UNFILTERED space. The obvious loop-until-short-page termination is therefore not a crash but silent data loss: it stops early and reports success. Drive offset to count() unconditionally. count() answered 35,156 on 2026-08-26 and only grows, so the real shape is roughly 71 sequential pages at limit 500.

Write both tests. The positive one proves the driver reaches count(). The negative one proves a naive implementation under-counts against the short-page fixture, so the trap cannot silently return via a future refactor that looks like a simplification.

Multicall does not help the page loop. One all(500, ...) already returns about 1.1 MB and dominates the eth_call budget; Onchain.Multicall.aggregate3/2 is for per-pool enrichment. Do not parallelise pagination with it.

limit: 500 is verified working against both the public https://mainnet.base.org and an Alchemy Base endpoint, so it is not a privileged-endpoint assumption. An endpoint with a tighter per-call gas or response cap can still refuse it; document that requirement rather than silently lowering the limit.

The remaining reads land in the same module and the same diff because they share the module, the signature plumbing and the fixture set; splitting them would force a second full cycle over one file for no coupling gain.

AUTHORITY: priv/abis/lp_sugar.json's all(uint256,uint256,uint256) signature and the task-4 fixtures, specifically the one demonstrating a non-zero filter returning a short page. Not velodrome-finance/sugar's README, which documents the stale two-argument all(limit, offset) that reverts on the deployed contract.

task.title: Bindings.RewardsSugar and Bindings.VeSugar
acceptance_criteria: RewardsSugar epochsLatest/3, epochsByAddress/4, rewards/4, rewardsByAddress/3 and forRoot/2 are implemented, decoding into [%Types.LpEpoch{}], [%Types.Reward{}] and a three-address tuple

task.body:
Port Slipstream's TickMath to pure Elixir and prove it equals the deployed Solidity — not by spot checks, but by sweeping the domain.

Base EVM simulation is blocked: onchain_evm's revm rejects chain id 8453. That is not a reason to weaken the evidence. A deployed pure-function oracle exists and is better than a local EVM. SlipstreamHelper.getSqrtRatioAtTick(int24) and getTickAtSqrtRatio(uint160) are pure, so a plain eth_call grades our port against real deployed bytecode. Multicall3 batching makes the full sweep cheap: roughly 1,775 aggregated calls, ten minutes of wall clock, once.

Three tiers of evidence, each doing a job the others cannot. The full-domain SHA-256 digest is 64 committed characters, impossible to satisfy by accident, and it is what makes the word swept true. The packed lattice makes a mismatch localisable to a tick instead of a shrug. The live boundary probes catch what in-range values cannot show you: revert behaviour, and int24 sign handling.

Implementation notes that will save a day. The Solidity port relies on truncating integer division and 128-bit right shifts, all fitting inside 256 bits with no intentional overflow, so Elixir bignums are safe — but never a float, and match the division semantics to the EVM operation in play: the unsigned getSqrtRatioAtTick pipeline uses truncating division (div/2), while getTickAtSqrtRatio's signed tail shifts with sar, which is FLOOR division — floor and truncate differ by one on negative intermediates, so a blanket div/2 port is off by one on the negative side there; use arithmetic right shifts (Bitwise) or explicit floor division for those steps. getTickAtSqrtRatio computes a most-significant-bit and a log base sqrt(1.0001) with signed intermediates, which is exactly where ports break; that is why the inverse fixture perturbs each ratio by plus and minus one.

The generator lives under lib/mix/tasks/ on purpose: Mix.Tasks.* resolves to no declared layer, so it may reach the network without violating the task-1 gate. Math.Tick itself must never call RPC, and after task 1 lands mix reach.check --arch will refuse it.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and report with measured numbers, not guesses: (a) if the binary fixture size draws an objection, gzip and gunzip at test time with :zlib — decide before generating; (b) measure the full-domain digest test's actual runtime and say whether it belongs inside mix ci or in its own alias; (c) confirm MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK from the deployed helper's own revert boundary rather than assuming Uniswap v3's values.

The liquidity half of Slipstream's math: converting between an L value plus a price range and the token amounts backing it. Analytics.Position and every valuation function downstream depend on this being exactly right, and exactly is not rhetorical — these functions carry a round-up flag precisely because a one-wei error in the wrong direction is a solvency bug upstream.

First, the deployed helper swaps sqrtRatioA and sqrtRatioB internally when they arrive out of order; a port that assumes A is less than B returns zeros for callers who pass upper-then-lower, and it will look like a data problem rather than a math problem. Second, getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta each have two overloads with different semantics — the uint128 plus round-up form, and the int128 signed form whose sign tracks mint against burn. Implement both. The signed form is not derivable from the unsigned one without care around negating the rounding.

task.body:
Aerodrome's v2 side has two curves and Lp.type picks between them: -1 is stable, 0 is volatile, and anything positive is a concentrated-liquidity tick spacing belonging to the tick-math modules. This task owns the two v2 curves.

The volatile curve is the ordinary constant product, and Onchain.DEX.Router.amount_out_v2/4 in onchain core already implements it. Use it as a cross-check, not as the implementation, because it takes fee in true basis points and Aerodrome's fee units need verifying separately.

The stable curve is Solidly's x^3*y + x*y^3, solved for the output side by Newton-Raphson on decimals-normalised reserves. Two things go wrong in every port: normalising to 18 decimals gets skipped (the invariant is not scale-invariant, so a 6-decimals token silently produces nonsense), and the iteration bound gets copied from a different fork.

The marginal-price function matters beyond quoting — it is what the price layer uses to price a token against a stable pool. Near balance, reserve1/reserve0 happens to be close to right, which is exactly why that bug survives review; it diverges precisely when the pool is imbalanced and the price is most interesting. The acceptance criterion for it is deliberately a test that would pass trivially against the naive version, so pick a fixture imbalanced enough that it does not.

task.body:
The shared vocabulary of the entire price layer: turning raw pool state into a Decimal price with token decimals handled correctly and exactly once.

Small module, outsized blast radius. Three consumers depend on it — Analytics.Price, Analytics.Pool and Sugar.Prices — and each would otherwise open-code the decimals adjustment, which is where token-decimals bugs live. A USDC/WETH pool priced without its 10^(6-18) correction is off by twelve orders of magnitude, which is obvious. A WBTC/WETH pool without its 10^(8-18) correction is off by ten, also obvious. A DAI/USDC pool is off by 10^12 and still looks like a number someone might believe.

Order of operations is load-bearing. Square the uint160 as an integer, then divide by 2 to the 192nd as a Decimal. Squaring a Decimal that has already been divided throws away half the significant digits. Money stays integer; only the ratio becomes Decimal.

The tick-consistency criterion exists so this module cannot drift from the tick oracle. Rather than testing against a hardcoded price table, it asserts that price-at-tick derived through our own verified sqrt_ratio_at_tick matches the mathematical definition. If task 13's port were wrong this test would not save you, but task 13 is graded against deployed bytecode, so the chain of authority holds.

OPEN DECISION to settle and name in the moduledoc: whether prices are canonically quoted as token1-per-token0 (the Uniswap convention, matching sqrtPriceX96 directly) or token0-per-token1. Pick one and make invert/1 the only way to get the other. A module that returns the price without saying which direction is a bug generator.

task.body:
This is the half of the price layer that must stay network-free, and its design exists specifically to make that possible. The package ships a built-in price source; the layer contract forbids analytics from making RPC calls. The resolution is that pricing is a pure function of a pool set plus a set of anchors — task 18 fetches them, this module turns them into prices. No .reach.exs layer change is needed: Math.Price is base, Types.Price is types, Analytics.Price is analytics, and the network lives one layer up in read.

Algorithm. Seed the map with the supplied anchors, typically Chainlink USD feeds plus a stablecoin. Then relax outward by breadth-first search over the pool graph, tokens as nodes and pools as edges, at most max_hops deep. At each step traverse only a pool whose TVL, computed in the numeraire from prices already resolved, clears the liquidity floor. Price each edge with spot/1, which dispatches on Lp.type. Record the route and the minimum pool TVL along it in the Price struct so a caller can judge the number rather than merely consume it.

Two ways this goes wrong quietly. Pricing a stable pool by the reserve ratio is correct near balance and badly wrong when imbalanced, which is exactly when someone is looking. And returning zero for a token nobody could price is worse: a zero propagates into TVL, into an APR denominator, and out the other end as an infinite yield. PriceMap therefore has no default — unpriceable tokens are enumerated with reasons and absent from the map.

Determinism is not a nicety. If the price map depends on the order Sugar happened to return pools in, then every downstream golden is flaky and every APR regression test becomes noise. Pin the tie-break and property-test it against shuffled inputs.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and record: (a) the default liquidity floor — sanity-check a candidate against the actual TVL distribution across the roughly 35,156 pools before writing it down as a default; (b) whether the numeraire is USD (anchored) or a stablecoin token, which differ whenever that stablecoin depegs. USD with the stablecoin treated as a priced token like any other makes a depeg visible instead of definitional.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1 defines the Lp struct this module consumes; the named fields in priv/abis/lp_sugar.json are the contract, and Lp.type is the discriminator. Fixtures must be real captured pages from that contract at a pinned block, not hand-written structs.

task.title: Bindings.Chainlink and Sugar.Prices — anchor feeds with a staleness policy, materialising a PriceMap
acceptance_criteria: Bindings.Chainlink latest_round_data/2, decimals/2 and description/2 wrap AggregatorV3Interface against a feed address, with the ABI captured into priv/abis/chainlink_aggregator_v3.json and its provenance recorded in priv/abis/README.md in the same table shape as the existing entries

The staleness policy returns an error rather than a number: a round older than max_staleness_s (defaulting to twice the feed's recorded heartbeat), or with a non-positive answer, or with answered_in_round behind round_id, yields a tagged error tuple. A unit test drives each rejection path with a synthetic round tuple

The staleness policy distinguishes a feed whose documented market hours have ended (updatedAt frozen, contract still callable — the tokenized-equity 24/5 case recorded in docs/protocol-context.md) from a feed that missed its heartbeat during expected publishing hours; those are different tagged errors, not one stale bucket. v0.1 default anchors remain crypto feeds; equity feeds are opt-in and must carry their market-hours policy and TRV-vs-raw unit as data on the Price, never as a silent exception to max_staleness_s

A stale or invalid anchor degrades explicitly — either the affected token lands in PriceMap.unpriced with :stale_anchor and the rest of the call succeeds, or the whole call fails. Whichever is chosen is documented and tested, and a stale anchor is NEVER silently replaced by a pool-derived price without the Price struct's source field reflecting that

task.body:
The network half of the price layer, and deliberately the only place in the price stack that touches a node.

Two sources, one output. Chainlink aggregators on Base give USD anchors for the major assets; the Aerodrome pool graph gives everything else by routing to those anchors. Both flow into Analytics.Price.resolve/3, which is pure. This module fetches and validates. If you find yourself multiplying prices here, the code belongs one layer down.

Chainlink has no FeedRegistry on Base, so feed addresses must be hardcoded, which makes verification the whole game. Every aggregator exposes description() returning a human string such as the pair name. Call it. An address that answers with the wrong pair, or does not answer at all, is caught immediately; an address copied from a stale doc page is caught no other way. Read decimals from the contract too — feeds are not uniformly 8.

Staleness is the failure mode that produces a confident wrong answer. latestRoundData will happily return a price from six hours ago during an outage, and every APR computed from it will look completely normal. Reject rather than report: an error tuple forces the caller to decide, a stale number does not.

Tokenized-equity Chainlink feeds on Base (Coinbase B20 stocks, live on Aerodrome as of 2026-08-24 — addresses and the 24/5 freeze behaviour are in docs/protocol-context.md) are a second, quieter form of the same trap. They report Total Return Value (underlying × B20 multiplier), publish 24/5, and hold the last value off-hours with updatedAt frozen while the contract stays callable. Crypto heartbeat logic that treats "callable + old updatedAt" as dead will false-red every weekend; logic that ignores updatedAt will settle against a Friday close. DEX pools for the same tokens trade 24/7, so Sunday spot versus a frozen TRV feed is allowed disagreement, not a routing bug. Pool reserves stay raw ERC-20; applying the B20 multiplier to them double-counts against a TRV feed. v0.1 ships crypto anchors. Equity feeds, if added, carry session calendar and unit as data on the Price.

The reconciliation test is the honest check on the whole design. If our pool-routed price for a token that also has a Chainlink feed disagrees with the feed beyond a small tolerance, either the routing is wrong or the pool is thin, and both are worth knowing before an APR denominator is built on it. Commit the comparison; do not tune the tolerance until it passes.

This task edits lib/onchain/aerodrome/contracts.ex, which tasks 19 and 25 also edit. Agree the key shape once — a suggested form is a feed lookup returning a map with address, description, decimals and heartbeat_s, rather than a bare address, so the staleness policy has data to work with.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and record: (a) which feeds ship in v0.1 — an ETH and a USDC feed are the minimum for a USD numeraire, and it is worth checking whether an AERO feed exists on Base at all, since it would let emission APR be USD-denominated without routing; equity feeds are not in that default set; (b) whether price_map/1 fetches the full roughly 71-page Lp enumeration or accepts a caller-supplied pool subset — full enumeration for a price map is enormously wasteful, so a subset with a documented default is probably right, but it interacts with task 23's pagination surface; (c) the partial-failure semantics named in the acceptance criteria.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Chainlink AggregatorV3 feeds on Base. Each one grades its own address through description(), decimals() and a live latestRoundData(). Cross-check against the provider's published Base feed list, but the deployed contract's own description() string is the authority; an explorer label alone is never sufficient, per this repo's address-verification rule.

task.body:
Pool-level valuation over an %Lp{} and a %PriceMap{}. Small surface, one genuinely unresolved question at its centre.

That question is fee units. Lp.pool_fee comes from Sugar, which sources it from two different factories with two different conventions: Aerodrome v2's PoolFactory expresses fees one way, and Slipstream's CLFactory expresses them in pips — 1e-6 units, the same scale as defaultUnstakedFee() at 100_000 for 10 percent. Whether Sugar normalises across the two, and what divisor applies to each, is not something to recall. Probe it. Take a known v2 pool and a known CL pool, read pool_fee from LpSugar, read the fee from the corresponding factory directly, and compare. Record the verified divisor per pool type in Contracts.constants() with the probe in the comment, exactly as the existing constants are documented. If Sugar's value turns out to need per-type interpretation, then fee_rate/1 must dispatch on pool_type/1 and a single shared divisor is a bug.

The TVL functions have a smaller but similar trap: a pool where only one token is priced. Returning the priced side's value as TVL halves the number and nothing complains. Return an error.

unstaked_fee_rate/1 is where the non-binary fee and emission split becomes computable. It is trivial arithmetic; its value is that task 21 has one verified place to get it from instead of re-deriving the pip conversion inline.

This task edits contracts.ex, shared with tasks 18 and 25. Coordinate so all three edits land in a compatible shape.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and record: (a) whether TVL for a CL pool uses reserve0/reserve1 (total across all ticks, which is what Sugar gives) or attempts an in-range figure — there is no in-range field in the Lp struct, so total is the only honest option, but it must be LABELLED as such because CL fee yield accrues only to in-range liquidity; (b) whether staked_tvl for a CL pool should use staked0/staked1 or gauge_liquidity — they are different units and task 21 needs both, so verify what staked0 and staked1 actually mean for a CL pool against a real gauged pool before either task assumes.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1 for Lp field semantics, the deployed CLFactory at 0x5e7BB104d84c7CB9B682AaC2F3d509f5F406809A for defaultUnstakedFee() (verified 100_000 pips) and tickSpacings() (verified [1, 50, 100, 200, 2000, 10]), and the deployed PoolFactory at 0x420DD381b31aEf6683db6B902084cB0FFECe40Da for the v2 fee convention. Probe them; do not infer fee units from documentation.

A test asserts that for at least 50 real captured positions, principal(position, lp.sqrt_ratio) reproduces the position's OWN amount0 and amount1 fields EXACTLY — Sugar computes those on-chain from the same inputs, so the golden page is simultaneously the input fixture and the expected output, and this differential costs no extra network call

Positions with zero liquidity and positions whose range lies entirely on one side of the current tick return correct single-sided or zero results rather than errors, with a fixture for each

Line coverage of Onchain.Aerodrome.Analytics.Position is at least 95 percent

task.body:
Position-level math over the 18-field %Position{} Sugar returns. The pleasant thing about this task is that its oracle is free: Sugar already computes amount0 and amount1 on-chain from the same liquidity and range our principal/2 uses, so a captured positions page is both the input fixture and the expected-output fixture. If the Math.Liquidity port is wrong in any way that matters, 50 real positions will say so without a single extra eth_call. Lead with that test.

The SlipstreamHelper.principal differential is the belt to that suspenders: it grades the same computation against a different deployed implementation and catches the case where Sugar and our port are wrong in the same direction.

Two semantics to establish by evidence rather than assumption. First, whether Position.liquidity is the position's total L or only its unstaked portion with staked holding the rest — the two readings give different staked fractions and both are plausible from the field names. Find a real partially-staked position and settle it; if none exists, compare a fully staked one against a fully unstaked one across liquidity, staked, amount0 and staked0. Second, the range-inclusion convention: pools treat the lower tick as inclusive and the upper as exclusive, so a position sitting exactly at its upper tick is out of range. Test both edges — this off-by-one mislabels precisely the positions that matter most.

unclaimed/3 returns a map, not a total, for the same reason APR returns separate rates: emissions_earned is denominated in the emissions token and the earned fees are denominated in the pool's two tokens. Summing them requires prices and a stated numeraire; the caller can do that deliberately with the PriceMap, and the signature should make it a choice rather than a default.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and document: (a) whether principal/2 should also offer an arity taking an %Lp{} directly, which is convenient but couples Position to Lp, or stay on the raw sqrt ratio, which is composable at the cost of one line at the call site; (b) how to represent a v2 position, which has no ticks at all — either Position analytics is CL-only with an explicit error for v2 rows, or principal/2 falls back to the LP-share proportion of reserves. Decide and document, because silently returning zeros for v2 positions is the failure mode.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1, whose positions() amount0 and amount1 outputs grade our principal computation, and the deployed SlipstreamHelper at 0x9c62ab10577fB3C20A22E231b7703Ed6D456CC7a. Both are on-chain; where our math disagrees with either, our math is wrong.

task.title: Analytics.APR — separate fee and emission rates, each carrying its denominator as data
acceptance_criteria: The return type is %Analytics.APR.Rate{} carrying at minimum kind (:fee or :emission), rate (Decimal), basis (an atom naming the denominator), numerator (with amount, unit, period and epochs_per_year 52), denominator (with amount, unit and label), and inputs recording the exact Lp, LpEpoch and price entries used. A bare Decimal is never returned from any APR function
Rate.combine/2 raises Analytics.APR.IncomparableBasisError whenever the two rates' basis values differ, and it is the ONLY combining function in the module's public API

Emission APR is computed from Lp.emissions times 604_800 — emissions is a PER-SECOND rate — annualised by Epoch.epochs_per_year/0 which is 52; a regression test asserts the produced rate is NOT equal to the daily-annualised variant, pinning out the roughly 7x error

emissions_cap is ALWAYS recorded in Rate.inputs and NEVER applied as a token-amount minimum. Live probing during roadmap review showed the gauge-factory cap mechanism is a RELATIVE share — defaultCap()/emissionsCaps() in basis points of MAX_BPS() on the gauge factories that expose it, with the other gauge factories reverting on those selectors (Sugar's _safe_emissions_cap then yields 0) — and Lp.emissions is the gauge's live post-notification reward rate, so whatever cap the protocol honours is already reflected in it and re-applying one double-counts. This task re-verifies that with its own recorded live probe against at least one cap-exposing and one reverting gauge factory, and sets Rate.capped from the probed factory semantics, with :unknown and a documented reason where the factory reverts. A grep test asserts no min() of a weekly emission against emissions_cap exists anywhere in the module

gauge_alive false yields {:unavailable, :gauge_not_alive} for the emission rate and NOT a zero rate; likewise {:unavailable, :no_gauge} for a zero gauge address and {:unavailable, :no_staked_liquidity} for a zero denominator. A test asserts a tagged tuple cannot be arithmetically combined with a Rate

Emission APR supports two bases and records which was used: a USD basis from staked0 and staked1 valued through a PriceMap, and a price-free basis of weekly emissions in emissions-token units over gauge_liquidity. The price-free basis is exercised by a test passing an EMPTY PriceMap and still succeeding

Fee APR is computed from an epoch-scoped fee flow taken from %LpEpoch{}.fees, NOT from Lp.token0_fees or Lp.token1_fees; those two are claimable balances accumulated over an unknown window, appear only in Rate.inputs, and the moduledoc states in one sentence why using them as a weekly flow is wrong

For CL pools the fee Rate carries a caveat marking that CL fees accrue to in-range liquidity only, as DATA on the struct and not merely as prose, because Sugar's reserves span all ticks and no in-range-only denominator is available

unstaked_cl_fee_apr/3 returns a Rate whose rate is the fee rate scaled by one minus Analytics.Pool.unstaked_fee_rate/1 and whose basis records that it is net of the unstaked fee; voter_fee_share/1 returns the complementary gauge rake; a test asserts the two partition the gross fee flow exactly
No function returns or accepts a float — a grep test enforces it — and all money stays integer until the final Decimal ratio
The module is pure: mix reach.check --arch passes under the task-1 rules
Line coverage of Onchain.Aerodrome.Analytics.APR is at least 95 percent
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Any total, blended or combined APR figure under any name — this is the point of the task
Reproducing the aerodrome.finance headline number; if ours differs the response is to state the denominators, never to tune a constant
Bribe or voting APR for veAERO holders — a different capital base, deliberately unfiled; file it via rmap new when veAERO-holder analytics is scoped
Historical APR series across epochs, which needs archive reads; v0.1 is current-epoch
The enforcement tests, goldens and coverage gate, which are task 22 and deliberately a different agent
task.body:
This is the module most likely to be silently wrong, because a wrong APR is still a plausible-looking number and nothing downstream will object to it. The brief is therefore not compute an APR but make it impossible to report one without its denominator.

The invariant: fee APR and emission APR are emitted separately, each tagged with its explicit denominator, and never summed. They are denominated over different capital bases; adding them is a category error, not an approximation. The mechanism is that neither function returns a number. Both return a %Rate{} carrying the rate, the basis, the numerator with its period and annualiser, the denominator with its unit, and the exact inputs used. Arithmetic on two structs raises. The only combining function that exists refuses mismatched bases. A caller who wants a single number has to reach into the rate field deliberately, at which point the choice is on the record in their code rather than in ours.

Four denominators to get right, each with a specific way of going wrong.

Emissions are PER SECOND. Weekly is emissions times 604_800. Annualising uses 52 epochs from Epoch.epochs_per_year/0. Annualising a daily figure by 365 overstates by roughly seven times and is the single most common error in this domain; there is a regression test for exactly that.

Emission APR is denominated in staked, in-range liquidity, not in total TVL. Support both the USD form and the price-free form. The price-free form is the honest primitive: it needs no oracle at all and cannot be wrong about a price.

emissions_cap is a trap, not a bound to apply. Where the gauge factories expose a cap at all it is a relative share in basis points of MAX_BPS(), not a token quantity, and several gauge factories revert on the cap selectors entirely. Lp.emissions is the post-notification rate the cap has already shaped. Record the cap as evidence in Rate.inputs; never subtract it from or min() it against the weekly rate.

Fee APR must come from an epoch-scoped flow. Lp.token0_fees and Lp.token1_fees are claimable balances that have been accumulating since someone last claimed, over an unknown window. Dividing them by a week produces a number whose error depends on claim behaviour, which is untraceable.

And the split is not binary on Slipstream. An unstaked concentrated-liquidity position still pays a rake to the gauge: CLFactory.defaultUnstakedFee() is 100_000 pips, which is 10 percent, per-pool overridable and surfaced as Lp.unstaked_fee. An unstaked CL LP keeps one minus that of trading fees, not all of them. Modelling this as a clean either/or understates voter revenue and overstates unstaked-CL yield.

Dead gauges return an unavailable tuple, not zero. Zero is a number: it averages, it charts, it ranks. A tagged tuple stops at the boundary and forces a decision.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and record: (a) what staked0 and staked1 actually mean for a CL pool — this must be settled jointly with task 19 against a real gauged pool, because it IS the emission denominator; (b) whether the USD emission basis atom should make the in-range caveat visible in the name itself; (c) whether the fee Rate for v2 pools uses reserves-TVL, which is available, or an epoch-average TVL, which is not available from a single Lp row — reserves-TVL with the limitation documented is the only honest option, so confirm it.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1 for emissions, emissions_cap, gauge_liquidity, staked0, staked1, unstaked_fee and gauge_alive; the deployed RewardsSugar at 0x1b121EfDaF4ABb8785a315C51D29BCE0552A7678 for WEEK() (verified 604800) and the LpEpoch fee flow; the deployed CLFactory at 0x5e7BB104d84c7CB9B682AaC2F3d509f5F406809A for defaultUnstakedFee() (verified 100_000); and the deployed Voter at 0x16613524e02ad97eDfeF371bC883F2F5d6C480A5 for cap and gauge-liveness semantics. The aerodrome.finance displayed APR is NOT an authority — it is a different denominator, and the correct response to a disagreement is to state which denominator each uses.

acceptance_criteria: A manifest test enumerates every exported function of every module under the Onchain.Aerodrome namespace via :application.get_key/2 and FAILS if any function name matches total_apr, combined_apr, overall_apr, net_apr, apr_sum or blended_apr. test/fixtures/goldens/apr/emission_apr_7_53.json is committed and records as explicitly NAMED fields: weekly_emissions_value 12337.58, epochs_per_year 52, denominator 8515374, denominator_basis, the pool address, the pinned block, the capture date, an expected rate of 0.0753, and a contrast block recording the aerodrome.finance displayed 8.76 percent together with a one-line note that the gap is the denominator and must never be closed by tuning a constant

Mutation-testing infrastructure beyond the assertions above
Reconciling against aerodrome.finance across many pools, which is not in v0.1
task.body:
Task 21 wrote the APR module. This task grades it, and it is assigned to a different agent on purpose: the agent that implemented a formula is the worst available judge of whether that formula is right.

Three things get made mechanical here, all of them domain truths that only the architect currently knows and that no per-task reviewer would independently catch.

First, the no-summing invariant. Documentation enforces nothing. Three overlapping mechanisms do: the return type is a struct so arithmetic on it raises; the only combining function refuses mismatched bases; and a manifest test walks the whole compiled module list and fails if anyone ever adds a function named like a blended APR. Note the anti-vacuity clauses in the criteria — a manifest test that silently scans zero modules is worse than no test, because it reports green. Assert the scan found something.

Second, the cross-check becomes a committed artefact rather than a sentence in a markdown file: 12337.58 times 52 over 8515374 is 7.53 percent, against a displayed 8.76 percent. The golden records the inputs AND the denominator AND the contrast, with a schema test on the golden itself so the denominator field cannot be dropped later. The two negative assertions matter as much as the positive one: the daily-annualised value pins out the roughly 7x error, and asserting we do NOT produce 8.76 percent documents in executable form that we are not trying to.

Third, coverage. The --cover-threshold flag is global only, but the JSON output carries a per-module array, so a small Mix task can enforce the tiered floors the house rules actually require: 95 percent for Analytics.* and Math.* because they are pure and there is no excuse, 80 percent elsewhere. The global threshold currently in mix.exs is a scaffold-time placeholder; replace it with a measured number and record what you measured.

If, while writing these, you find that an APR formula is wrong, file it as a new task and say so plainly in the write-up. Do not fix it here. The separation between implementing and grading is the whole reason this task exists as its own dispatch.

DISPATCH NOTE: the coverage-gate half gives this task a repo-wide effective write-set — every module's coverage becomes a landing-time invariant — so dispatch it as a SOLO wave; nothing lands in parallel with it.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1 and RewardsSugar at 0x1b121EfDaF4ABb8785a315C51D29BCE0552A7678 supply the golden's inputs at a pinned block — capture them live rather than transcribing them. The consumer-facing pool and token read API — the most visible surface in the package, and the one an agent or a human actually calls.

This is the ground-truth correction most likely to be quietly fixed into an account-scoping assumption by a future refactor if the naming here is ambiguous.

Capturing governance-only Voter setters
Any address for a chain other than Base
task.body:
Capture the ABIs and verify the addresses for the three contracts the full write surface needs and that are entirely absent from this repo today: the Aerodrome Router (swap and v2 liquidity), the Slipstream NonfungiblePositionManager (CL position lifecycle), and the Gauge contracts (stake, unstake, claim).

Follow the Sourcify v2 capture protocol already documented in priv/abis/README.md exactly. Do not deviate from it, and do not accept a null or partial Sourcify match without flagging it — all nine existing entries resolved with both creationMatch and runtimeMatch non-null, and a new entry that does not should be visible, not smoothed over.

Address discovery is where this task earns its score. Do not trust an explorer label. Cross-reference the Sugar team's own base.env deployment manifest, AND run a live cast call against each candidate for a view function whose expected return you can state in advance. Then use the fact that Sugar's Lp struct carries nfpm and gauge per pool: pull a live row and confirm the addresses agree. That third check is nearly free once you have any working eth_call, and it is the one that catches a manifest that has drifted.

Every downstream write task inherits these addresses. A wrong one here does not fail loudly; it produces calldata aimed at the wrong contract.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Router, NFPM and Gauge contracts on Base at the addresses this task discovers and verifies. Not the Sugar README, not a BaseScan label, not any assumption about what the Router should look like. A captured ABI is correct if and only if it matches the bytecode actually live at that address, confirmed by non-null Sourcify match fields and by at least one live eth_call that only the real contract could answer correctly.

task.title: Golden-calldata evidence harness: an independent cast oracle plus eth_call impersonation, proven on Voter
acceptance_criteria: A CalldataFixture test helper shells out to the local Foundry cast binary to produce REFERENCE calldata for a given signature and arguments, and that reference — never our own Onchain.ABI.encode_call/2 output — is what assertions compare against
If cast is not on PATH the test FLUNKS, never skips, naming the exact install command

A second helper performs eth_call-as-impersonation: it sets the JSON-RPC from field to a real address discovered through a Sugar read, obtaining a genuine simulated return value or revert reason from the deployed contract without that address's private key and without broadcasting anything

A demonstration test against Voter reset(uint256) — whose ABI is already captured, so this task does not depend on task 25 — proves the golden assertion byte-exact against cast calldata output, AND a negative-control eth_call against the deployed Voter with a veNFT id the impersonated address does not own returns a real, SPECIFIC on-chain revert rather than a generic execution-reverted string

The helper's @doc states in one paragraph what this evidence model CANNOT prove — that a state-mutating call actually succeeds and commits on-chain — and why: Base simulation is blocked and broadcasting a real transaction is out of scope for a test suite
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Router, Gauge and NFPM specific tests, which land with each contract's write task reusing this harness
Signing or broadcasting any transaction
eth_call state-override tricks, which are non-portable per node-portability rule 1 and explicitly not used here
task.body:
This is the shared piece every write task depends on, and it must exist before those tasks write a single test that grades our encoder against our encoder — which is a false green, not weak evidence.

Build two things.

First, an independent encoder oracle. Shell out to Foundry's cast to encode the same call the library encodes, and assert byte-for-byte equality. cast is a different codebase in a different language implementing the same ABI specification, which is what makes it an oracle rather than a mirror.

Second, eth_call impersonation. The from parameter of eth_call lets you simulate a call as if any address sent it, without owning that address's key and without broadcasting, because eth_call never mutates state or requires a valid signature. Use it for real positive evidence (a decoded return from a state-mutating function's simulated execution) or real negative evidence (a specific revert from crafted bad inputs) straight from the deployed bytecode.

Prove the whole harness end to end against Voter.reset(uint256), whose ABI is already captured, so this task is not blocked on task 25.

Be honest in the docs about the ceiling. With Base simulation blocked, no test here can prove a write succeeds and commits. Say so, once, plainly, rather than letting a reader infer more from a green suite than it can support.

AUTHORITY: Foundry's cast, independently implementing ABI encoding, is the oracle for calldata-shape correctness. The deployed Voter at 0x16613524e02ad97eDfeF371bC883F2F5d6C480A5, verified in priv/abis/README.md on 2026-08-26, is the oracle for on-chain revert semantics. Neither is this repo's own encoder.

A completeness test derives the covered-function set from the ABI JSON minus an explicit named-exclusion list, so a re-captured ABI that adds a write function fails the test instead of being silently absent
Every function returns {:ok, %{to: address, calldata: binary}} BY DEFAULT with no signing and no key material touched

An opt-in signer option threads to Onchain.Signer, and it is impossible to reach a signing path without an explicit caller-supplied signer; a grep test asserts no System.get_env call in this module reads anything key-shaped
vote's pools and weights array-length mismatch is checked locally before encoding and returns a tagged error tuple, saving a wasted round-trip on a bug the contract also rejects
Golden-calldata tests pass the task-26 cast oracle for vote, reset and claimBribes — representative of scalar, single-argument and nested-array argument shapes
A negative-control eth_call against the deployed Voter with a veNFT id the impersonated address does not own returns real on-chain reverts for BOTH reset and vote
Governance-only setters are explicitly out of scope and the moduledoc says why they are not a library concern

updateFor and notifyRewardAmount — keeper and minter accounting entrypoints with no library consumer; they go on the completeness test's explicit exclusion list with that reason, never silently omitted
veNFT ownership and eligibility reads, which are the read layer
Any dependency on task 25 — voter.json is already captured, and adding one would be a spurious dependency
task.body:
Build the write surface for the already-captured Voter contract. This is deliberately the first write module, because its ABI provenance is already settled — priv/abis/README.md carries its row and its live probe — so it does not wait on task 25 and it validates the task-26 harness against a real contract early.

Low risk on provenance does not mean low stakes. Misdirected votes cost a whole epoch of emission weighting, and vote takes parallel arrays whose length mismatch is exactly the kind of caller bug worth catching before it becomes an on-chain revert someone paid gas for. Check it locally, and still test that the contract rejects it too.

Writes return calldata. Signing is opt-in and requires an explicit signer; no module in this package reads a private key from the environment on its own.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Voter at 0x16613524e02ad97eDfeF371bC883F2F5d6C480A5, verified 2026-08-26. Its ownership-check reverts on reset and vote grade this task, and Foundry's cast grades the calldata shape.

task.title: Write.Router — swap and liquidity calldata builders with Signer opt-in
acceptance_criteria: Swap functions over Aerodrome's four-field Route struct — Solidly's (from, to, stable) plus the factory field Aerodrome added, which the encoder must include — and addLiquidity and removeLiquidity (stable is a bool parameter on each; the actual signature variants are the ETH forms), all returning {:ok, %{to: address, calldata: binary}} by default
An opt-in signer option threads to Onchain.Signer; a grep test asserts no System.get_env call in this module reads anything key-shaped
Golden-calldata tests pass the task-26 cast oracle for a single-hop swap, a multi-hop swap, a stable-pool liquidity call and a volatile-pool liquidity call

A negative-control eth_call against the deployed Router with an intentionally expired deadline returns the real on-chain expiry revert, proving deadline enforcement is contract-side and not encoder-side
A second negative control with a slippage minimum set above any achievable output returns the real insufficient-amount revert

The stable boolean is treated as a domain invariant, not a flag: a test asserts that flipping it targets a DIFFERENT deployed pool for the same token pair, because a wrong default here silently routes to the wrong pool

The @doc states explicitly whether route validity is checked locally before encoding or left to the contract to revert on, and that this module does not compute expected LP amounts or fair slippage minimums — those are analytics concerns, named as a handoff
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Router-side quoting such as quoteAddLiquidity — a read concern, deliberately unfiled; file it via rmap new when a consumer needs in-package quoting
Computing a fair slippage minimum — an analytics concern, deliberately unfiled; file it via rmap new alongside router quoting when swap-safety analytics is scoped
Concentrated-liquidity position management, which is task 30
task.body:
The Router write surface: swaps and v2 liquidity provision, in one module and one dispatch because they share a file and a deadline discipline, and separating them would sequence two full cycles over one file.

Swap calldata is the easiest write to get subtly wrong — route ordering, and the stable flag on each hop — and the failure mode is that a caller trusts calldata encoding the wrong route. The stable boolean deserves the sharpest test in this task: it selects between two entirely different deployed pools for the same token pair, mirroring the Lp.type discriminator, so wrong flag equals wrong pool. Assert it against real deployed addresses, not against our own routing logic.

Every function takes a deadline. Treat never-a-stale-deadline as a domain invariant worth an explicit negative control rather than something exercised incidentally.

This module does not compute expected amounts or a fair slippage minimum. It takes caller-supplied minimums as-is and says so in the @doc, so nobody mistakes it for a safety layer it is not.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Router at the address task 25 verifies — specifically its revert behaviour on a crafted expired-deadline eth_call and on a slippage-minimum breach — grades this task. Not our own encoder, and not the Solidly or Velodrome reference implementation source, which is reference material only.

Reward-token discovery, which RewardsSugar covers
Voter-side claiming, which is task 27

The gauge write surface: staking and unstaking LP positions, and claiming rewards. This is the smallest of the four write contracts by function count. Do not pad it with speculative functions the captured ABI does not actually expose, and do not assume the function names — read them from the capture.

The one real branch is whether Slipstream CL gauges and v2 gauges share a selector set. Task 25 answers that; honour whichever answer it recorded rather than assuming one shape covers both, because a v2-shaped call against a CL gauge fails at the worst possible moment.

Writes return calldata; signing is opt-in with an explicit signer.

AUTHORITY: a real deployed Gauge instance, its address obtained from a live Lp.gauge read per task 25's cross-check. Its revert on an over-withdraw grades this task; Foundry's cast grades the calldata shape.

task.title: Write.NFPM — Slipstream concentrated-liquidity position lifecycle
acceptance_criteria: mint, increaseLiquidity, decreaseLiquidity and collect all return calldata by default with the same Signer opt-in contract; a grep test asserts no System.get_env call reads anything key-shaped

mint's tick-range arguments are validated against Contracts.constants().tick_spacings before encoding, and the @doc states that this local check is a courtesy to save wasted gas and NEVER a substitute for the contract's own enforcement
Golden-calldata tests pass the task-26 cast oracle for mint and for at least one of increase, decrease or collect

A negative-control eth_call against the deployed NFPM with a tick range outside the pool's spacing — deliberately bypassing the local check — returns a real on-chain revert, testing the contract's own defence rather than ours
Position closing (decrease to zero, collect, then burn) is either implemented alongside collect, since the three are tightly coupled, or explicitly named out of scope with a one-line reason
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Position discovery and enumeration, which the read layer covers
Tick-to-price conversion math, which lives in Math.Tick and Math.Price
Computing a fair slippage minimum for a mint, which is an analytics concern
task.body:
The write surface for Slipstream concentrated-liquidity position lifecycle management through the NonfungiblePositionManager. This is the most parameter-dense write surface in the package: mint alone carries tick bounds, the pool-identifying tickSpacing — Slipstream's MintParams has NO fee field; the pool key is (token0, token1, tickSpacing), and sqrtPriceX96 in MintParams creates the pool when it does not yet exist — both token amounts and their minimums, a recipient and a deadline.

Resist the temptation to under-validate mint's tick arguments on the grounds that the contract will revert anyway. A caller deserves a cheap local check before spending gas on a doomed transaction. But that check must never become load-bearing in place of the real on-chain enforcement, which is why the acceptance criteria require testing both: the local rejection, and the deployed revert when the local check is deliberately bypassed.

Writes return calldata; signing is opt-in with an explicit signer.

AUTHORITY: the deployed NFPM at the address task 25 verifies, specifically its revert on an out-of-spacing tick range via a crafted eth_call. Not this module's own local pre-check, and not any remembered Uniswap v3 NFPM interface — Slipstream's differs.

task.title: Mutation-survivor audit: prove the golden-calldata comparators actually discriminate
acceptance_criteria: For every Write.* golden-calldata test added in tasks 27 through 30, a paired canary test deliberately corrupts one byte or one argument of the expected calldata and asserts the comparator DOES fail on the corrupted value, proving the assertion is exact-byte equality rather than a prefix match, a length-only check, or an accidentally-true comparison
At least one canary targets a nested array argument such as Voter vote(uint256,address[],uint256[]), since array-encoding offset and length fields are the most common place a looks-equal bug hides
The audit is a REUSABLE helper used identically across all four write modules, not one-off corruption code copy-pasted per test file

A doc note states that this substitutes for real mutation-testing tooling, since no established Elixir mutation-testing framework is in the dependency set, and names what would replace it if one became available
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Adopting a general-purpose Elixir mutation-testing library, which is a separate and larger decision
Mutating anything other than the golden-calldata assertions — analytics mutation grading is task 22's territory
Changing any write module's encoding; a defect found here is filed as a new task
task.body:
This closes the gap the onchain-verification discipline calls a deliberate negative control and mutation-survivor review, without pretending real mutation-testing tooling exists here. It does not, and Base simulation is blocked, so building a mutation framework from scratch is out of proportion to this milestone.

Instead, build the minimal thing that actually proves the golden tests have discriminating power: deliberately break one byte of the known-correct calldata per function and confirm the suite notices. A golden test that would pass against garbage is worse than no test, because it reports coverage it does not have.

Nested-array arguments get their own canary. Offset and length fields in ABI array encoding are where a comparator that only checks a prefix or a length silently agrees with a wrong value.

If a canary reveals that a write module's encoding is actually wrong, file it as a new task and say so. Do not fix it here — this task grades comparators, it does not re-implement encoders.

ROUTING: this audit is routed to codex for evaluator separation — cursor and grok are one model family, and tasks 27 through 29 were implemented by that family; codex overlaps only with task 30's comparator, and the write-up must name that residual self-audit rather than letting it pass as fully independent.

AUTHORITY: the cast reference values established in tasks 26 through 30 are the ground truth being mutated against. This task's job is proving the comparator, not re-deriving correctness.

task.title: Runnable ABI-drift detector: re-fetch every priv/abis entry and diff selector sets
acceptance_criteria: An integration-tagged test iterates every row of priv/abis/README.md's captured-files table, re-runs its EXACT RECORDED curl against live Sourcify — not a command reconstructed from the address — and asserts the 4-byte function-selector set of the fresh fetch equals the selector set of the committed JSON file
On a mismatch the failure message lists exactly which selectors were added, removed or changed, so the report is actionable rather than a bare drift-detected
The test also asserts that match, creationMatch and runtimeMatch are still non-null on the fresh fetch, catching a regression to a partial or unverified match and not only a selector change
It never skips on unreachable Sourcify; it flunks naming the exact endpoint URL

Selector-level comparison is used deliberately rather than whole-ABI equality, and the moduledoc says why: harmless metadata and ordering differences must not false-positive, while a selector-set change is what actually breaks a caller

A one-paragraph note states that decode-level drift — a field silently becoming nil because components were reordered — is the types layer's concern, covered by the field-order tests in tasks 6 and 7, and names that handoff rather than silently omitting it
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Struct-decode-level drift detection, which tasks 6 and 7 own
Auto-remediation: this detector reports, a human re-captures
Contracts outside priv/abis
task.body:
Sugar drift is the standing hazard in this package, and the current defence is a paragraph of advice in CLAUDE.md. Build the runnable thing instead.

Every entry in priv/abis/README.md already records the exact curl that produced it. Reuse that recorded command verbatim rather than reconstructing it from the address — the recorded command is the artifact under test, and a reconstruction that happens to work hides a README that has rotted.

Compare selector sets, not whole ABIs. Docstring and ordering differences are noise; a changed, added or removed selector is what actually breaks a caller. And check the match fields too: a contract that silently regresses from an exact match to a partial one is drift of a different kind, and this is the only place it would surface.

AUTHORITY: live Sourcify v2, queried with the exact recorded curl, is the sole authority on whether the deployed ABI has drifted. Not the Sugar team's README — which is already proven stale on the all/2 versus all/3 signature — and not this repo's own committed JSON.

task.title: Live integration proof of the full read, analytics and price surface across two endpoints
acceptance_criteria: An integration-tagged suite exercises Sugar.Pools, Sugar.Tokens, Sugar.Positions, Sugar.VeNfts, Sugar.Rewards, Sugar.Relays and Sugar.Prices against a live Base RPC, excluded from the default mix test.json run and from mix ci's excluded-integration pass

At least one assertion proves the FULL Sugar.Pools enumeration reaches or exceeds a live count() call made in the same test — the end-to-end proof that the pagination driver behaves against the real contract and not only against fixtures

The suite runs through the task-5 multi-endpoint seam and asserts identical decoded results from the public Base endpoint and a second unprivileged provider, so the portability claim rests on two endpoints rather than one

At least one Analytics.APR result is computed end to end from live data and asserted for INTERNAL consistency: each Rate's numerator over its denominator reproduces its rate, and the fee and emission bases differ. No assertion compares against aerodrome.finance

The suite doc states explicitly that this is NOT a revm or fork simulation, since Base chain id 8453 is hard-blocked in onchain_evm, and that it is a live-endpoint proof complementing the pinned-fixture suite rather than replacing it
Missing credentials flunk with the exact env vars and export commands; nothing is ever skipped silently
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Write-path testing, which is milestone v0_2
Anything requiring EVM simulation
Tuning any analytics constant to match a frontend figure
task.body:
The proof that the v0.1 surface works end to end against live Base state, not only against golden fixtures.

Run every Sugar module against a real endpoint and assert at least one cross-checkable invariant per module. The load-bearing one is pagination: enumerate fully and compare against a live count() made in the same test. Fixtures prove the decoder; only this proves the loop.

Route everything through the task-5 seam. Green against our own endpoint alone proves nothing about portability — the consumer's node, not ours, is the case that matters, and the identical green run on both endpoints is what the portability claim rests on.

Do not attempt an Onchain.EVM fork test. Base is hard-blocked in onchain_evm's revm binding, and a test that cannot run is worse than an absent one because it reads as coverage.

For analytics, assert internal consistency only: that each Rate reproduces its own numerator over its own denominator and that the two bases differ. Deliberately assert nothing about the frontend's displayed figure. If ours disagrees, the correct response is to state which denominator each uses, not to tune a constant.

AUTHORITY: live Base RPC responses at whatever block the run happens against, from the addresses in lib/onchain/aerodrome/contracts.ex, across two independent endpoints. This is the complement to the pinned-fixture suite, not a replacement for it.

acceptance_criteria: CHANGELOG.md's Unreleased section becomes a dated 0.1.0 entry enumerating the real shipped surface — types, bindings, pure math, the price layer, analytics and the Sugar read API — rather than a copy of roadmap task titles
README.md's scaffold status line is replaced with an accurate statement of what is actually implemented, or explicitly kept with a one-line reason if something in v0_1 did not land

The task write-up records, as a non-task operator prerequisite, that onchain_aerodrome is not yet registered in the harness project registry while every sibling onchain repo is, with check_command mix check.dispatch, landing_policy auto and target_branch main

Registering the repo in the harness project registry, which is an operator action and not a file change
Any API-stability commitment beyond 0.1.0
The write surface, which ships in v0_2
task.body:
The capstone for v0_1. Everything else in the milestone has to be true before this closes, and its job is to make the gap between mix ci is green and this is a real consumable hex package disappear.

Three things carry weight beyond bookkeeping.
